coverage.concept: Robustness and validation strategies: inline filtering, string parsing, and formatted extraction with checks
Formatted extraction skips leading whitespace, consumes a valid prefix, leaves delimiters, and uses buffered input before waiting
Four input problem categories: meaningless values, extra characters, parse failure, and numeric overflow
Application-level validation and retry loops for calculator operators; successful extraction is not sufficient
Discard through newline with ignore and numeric_limits<streamsize>::max; fixed counts can leave input behind

Persistent failure state, fail() and Boolean conversion, invalid conversion values, and clear-before-ignore recovery
EOF is a state rather than a character; terminal requests, disconnected input, termination, and successful final tokens

steps.title: Trace buffered input and choose a suffix policy
steps.objective: Predict prefix extraction and distinguish discarding a suffix from rejecting it.
steps.explanation:
Formatted operator>> skips leading spaces, tabs, and newlines, consumes a convertible prefix, and leaves unrelated characters buffered. Later reads use those characters before waiting for new input; printing prompts does not empty the buffer. Thus a calculator can consume an entire expression entered at its first prompt, making subsequent prompts run together.

Choose a policy: accept the prefix and discard the suffix, or reject extra input. After successful extraction, the source's strict test is !input.eof() && input.peek() != '\n', equivalently !(input.eof() || input.peek() == '\n'). peek observes without consuming. This rejects even trailing spaces, accepts a newline or already-reached EOF, and must follow the extraction-success check. The workspace uses the permissive policy.

Source: [LearnCpp 9.5, extraction recap, sample calculator, and Error case 2](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/stdcin-and-handling-invalid-input/). Alex's article (updated January 29, 2025) has demonstrations but no quiz or explicit coding assignments; these activities are supplementary.

questions.question: Which two lines are printed?
questions.explanation: The first extraction leaves *9 and the newline buffered. peek observes * without consuming it; the next two extractions obtain * and 9.

steps.title: Separate conversion from meaning
steps.objective: Choose validation checks for conversion, application rules, and a complete calculation.
steps.explanation:
Robust programs give unexpected input a defined outcome. Validation can filter keystrokes in a suitable interface, read text then parse it, or attempt formatted extraction and check the result. std::cin does not provide per-keystroke filtering. Extracting a string avoids numeric conversion but still needs parsing and stream checks; operator>> reads a word, not a whole line, and can fail at EOF.

Consider four problems: meaningless values, leftovers, conversion failure, and numeric overflow. A successfully extracted k still fails the calculator's +, -, *, / rule: reject it, explain, and retry unless input ends. Likewise, zero is convertible but invalid as a division denominator: request another denominator, not another numerator. Keep a defensive result-function fallback for unexpected operators or invalid division even when the normal input path validates them.

Source: [LearnCpp 9.5, Validating input, Types of invalid text input, Error case 1, and Putting it all together](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/stdcin-and-handling-invalid-input/). Later source examples may omit validation for focus; that does not establish robust behavior.

steps.title: Make the next read start after this line
steps.objective: Implement a reusable line-discard helper without a fragile character limit.
steps.explanation:
Implement discardLine(std::istream& input) for a stream that is not in failure state. Remove everything through the next newline, including that newline, or through end-of-input. Preserve the following line.

Use ignore with std::numeric_limits<std::streamsize>::max() from <limits>; this special count disables the count limit, whereas a fixed 100 can leave a long suffix behind. std::istream& lets the helper accept std::cin or simulated input; this mini uses only simulated input.

Source: [LearnCpp 9.5, Error case 2 and ignoreLine demonstration](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/stdcin-and-handling-invalid-input/).

hints: ignore(count, delimiter) removes the delimiter too when it finds one.
Use std::streamsize for the numeric_limits type, not int.
The helper operates on input, not on the global std::cin.
examples: Input "trailing words\n42\n": after discardLine, the next integer is 42.
Input "\n42": remove just the initial newline, leaving 42.
Input "trailing words" with no newline: consume it all and reach EOF.

steps.title: Repair state before removing bad input
steps.objective: Recover from invalid text and overflow without trusting failed destinations.
steps.explanation:
An integer conversion encountering a letter stores zero, leaves the letter buffered, and sets failbit. input.fail() or !input detects failure; subsequent reads and ignore cannot proceed. For recoverable failures, clear() first, then ignore through newline. Clearing alone leaves the bad input; ignoring first leaves it too. Check EOF before clearing, and remember conversion success before unconditional cleanup changes the state.

Numeric overflow uses the same failure path: extraction clamps to the nearest representable boundary and sets failbit, rather than wrapping or accepting the value. The source's 16-bit example reads 40000 as 32767 and blocks later reads, despite its misleading 'extraction succeeds' heading. A later blocked extraction leaves its destination unchanged. By contrast, 21 fits int but violates the workspace's [1,20] rule without stream failure.

Source: [LearnCpp 9.5, Error cases 3 and 4](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/stdcin-and-handling-invalid-input/).

questions.question: Which three lines are printed?
questions.explanation: The failed conversion stores zero. The first ignore cannot act on the failed stream. After clear(), o is still present. The second ignore removes the bad line so the next read gets 17.

steps.title: Build a finite, reusable number reader
steps.objective: Combine success-first handling, recoverable failure cleanup, suffix discard, and EOF termination.
steps.explanation:
EOF is a state, not a character; a live terminal normally waits for input. End-of-input requests commonly use Ctrl-D on Unix or Ctrl-Z then Enter on Windows, with terminal-specific behavior for pending text. eof() reports an operation reaching the end, not future read success. Clearing an exhausted or disconnected source cannot create data. Crucially, a final integer without a newline can set eofbit without failbit: Boolean conversion stays true, so process that value before any failed-read EOF path.

Implement bool readNumber(std::istream& input, int& result), without prompts. Read into a temporary; on success, discard the suffix, assign result, and return true. Accept every representable int, including zero, negatives, and final tokens without newlines. On failed extraction at EOF, return false with result unchanged; otherwise clear, discard the failed line, and retry. Use ordinary streams with default exception settings and recoverable text/overflow failures.

Source: [LearnCpp 9.5, Error cases 2–4, Checking for EOF, and Putting it all together](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/stdcin-and-handling-invalid-input/), plus the [workspace's final-token requirement](workspaces/09/09_05/lesson.md). The source helper exits on failed-read EOF; this reusable reader reports false instead.
steps.sourceExercise: supplementary — EOF discussion and new reader activity combining ignoreLine, clearFailedExtraction, and getDouble demonstrations; bool return replaces process exit; final-token semantics follow workspace notes

hints: Use if (input >> candidate) to handle success before considering EOF.
On failed extraction, stop at EOF. Otherwise clear() before ignore(max, '\n'), then retry.
Only assign result after a successful conversion. Do not decide whether it succeeded by checking state after ignore().
Discard the successful line's suffix too, so another call starts on the next line.
examples: Input "oops\n-6 extra\n": return true and set result to -6.
Input "0" with no final newline: return true and set result to 0.
Empty input with result initially 314: return false and leave result equal to 314.
An overflowing integer followed by a line containing 11: recover and return 11, not the clamped boundary.

steps.title: Finish the workspace quantity reader
steps.objective: Implement the existing quantity contract with finite recovery and correct EOF behavior.
steps.explanation:
Open the [workspace notes](workspaces/09/09_05/lesson.md) and [main.cpp](workspaces/09/09_05/main.cpp). Implement readQuantity() with std::cin and no prompts: return the first integer in [1,20], discarding each attempt's suffix. Retry after invalid text, overflow, or out-of-range values; return -1 if input ends before a valid quantity. Accept 3 extra as 3 and final 20 without a newline as 20. Formatted extraction may skip blank leading whitespace.

Predict hello
0
8
 → 8, 21
1
 → 1, empty input → -1, and final 20 → 20. Run the retained tests before and after implementation, then add one boundary case, such as final out-of-range input without a newline. Explain clear-before-ignore and success-before-EOF. The scaffold supplies simulated input; submit with ./course check 9.5.
